full_judgment:
Mirza Hussain Haider J. Civil Appeal No. 375 of 2009 by leave and Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 216 of 2008 are directed against the judgment and order dated 10.12.2007, passed by the High Court Division in First Miscellaneous Appeal Nos. 86 of 2006 and 145 of 2007 respectively, allowing both the appeals and disposing of the connected Civil Rule Nos. 803(FM) of 2005 and 795(FM) of 2005 and thereby setting aside the judgment and order dated 21.5.2005 passed by the Fourth Artharin Adalat, Dhaka, in Miscellaneous Case Nos. 36 of 2003 and 35 of 2003 respectively filed under Order XXI Rule 58 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. Since the facts and circumstances of both the cases are similar and the facts of Civil Appeal No. 375 of 2009 will govern Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 216 of 2008, as such the fact of Civil Appeal No. 375 of 2009 is narrated in short below:

3. That the present respondent No.2 (National Bank Limited) as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 32 of 1989 in the then Court of Subordinate Judge and First Commercial Court, Dhaka, against M/S. Cosmopolitan Trading Corporation and Abul Hossain (present respondent No. 3 and predecessor of present proforma respondent Nos. 4 to 13 of Civil Appeal No. 375 of 2009 respectively, who are also present respondent No. 23 and predecessor of present proforma respondent Nos. 24 to 33 of Civil Petition No. 216 of 2008 (respectively) as defendants for realization of loan, with interest, amounting to TK.38,91,338.00 stating inter alia that the present respondent No.3 M/s. Cosmopolitan Trading Corporation, for the purpose of its business, took loan of TK. 25,00,000/- from the plaintiff bank and Abul Hossain, the predecessor of the present respondent Nos. 4 to 13, signed the guarantee form as guarantor upon mortgaging the property as described in the schedule to the plaint alleging that Abul Hossain, the full brother of Dr. Abdul Mannan being appointed as the attorney of Dr. Abdul Mannan by registered Power of Attorney dated 23.10.1983 mortgaged 2.375 acres of land of SA Plot No. 2029 and 1.20 acres of land of SA Plot No. 91 to the plaintiff bank against the loan obtained by M/S. Cosmopolitan Trading Corporation belonging to Abdul Kader Patwari father-in-law of the said Abul Hossain. The said M/S. Cosmopolitan Trading Corporation having failed to repay the loan the bank instituted the said suit. The said suit was subsequently transferred to the Fourth Artharin Adalat, Dhaka and renumbered as Title Suit No. 177 of 1998 and was ultimately decreed ex parte by judgment and decree dated 8.4.2001. Thereaft6r, the plaintiff bank put the said decree into execution vide Title Execution Case No. 37 of 2002 in the First Additional Artharin Adalat, Dhaka. The said execution case was subsequently transferred to the Fourth Artharin Adalat, Dhaka and renumbered as Execution Case No. 1242 of 2003. Since Md. Abul Hossain, the constituted attorney of Dr. Abdul Mannan, the owner of the property under mortgage, died and Dr. Abdul Mannan himself also died earlier, the present appellant, Mohammad Zahangir Alam, was added in the execution case as judgment debtor being heir of late Dr. Abdul Mannan.

4. The present respondent No.1 (Concord Condominium Limited) having come to know about inclusion of its purchased property in the schedule of the Money Execution Case No. 37 of 2002, filed an application under Order XXI Rule 58 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure as third party, which was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 36 of 2003. It is stated in the said application that Dr. Abdul Mannan, the owner, by purchase, of 2.375 acres of land appertaining to CS and SA Plot No. 2029 of Mouza-Uttar Kaundia, P.S. Savar, Dhaka, who subsequently, out of the aforesaid 2.3750 acres of land, transferred 1.00 acre of land to Abdul Baten and Md. Abul Kashem by registered Deed No. 3166 dated 4.4.1994 and on the same day also he transferred 1.00 acre of land to Haji Md. Ahsan Ullah and Asia Begum by registered Deed No. 3167 dated 4.4.1994 and thereafter he transferred 0.3750 acre of land to Md. Ohidul Islam by registered Deed No. 3976 dated 27.4.1994 and as such he exhausted his entire share in the said plot. All the aforesaid transfer deeds were executed and registered by one Fazlul Hoque, the constituted attorney of Dr. Abdul Mannan. That all the aforesaid purchasers, in their turn, transferred the entire 2.375 acres of land to the present respondent No.1 (Concord Condomonium Limited) by three registered Deeds bearing Nos. 7789, 11111 and 15076 dated 7.7.1996, 9.9.1996 and 24.11.1996 respectively and since then the same has been in possession and enjoyment of the present respondent No.1 who got its name mutated and is paying rents in accordance with law.

5. On the other hand, the present respondent Nos. 1 to 21 of Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 216 of 2008 having come to know about the said ex parte decree and inclusion of their purchased property in the schedule of the Money Execution Case No. 37 of 2002 also filed Miscellaneous Case No. 35 of 2003 under Order XXI Rule 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure stating that Dr. Abdul Mannan, owner by purchase, of 1.1315 acres of land appertaining to SA Plot No. 91 of Mouza-Ranchandrapur, PS.  Mohammadpur, District-Dhaka, transferred .8750 acre of land out of the said 1.1315 acres of land, to Md. Abdul Baten and Md. Shahjahan Miah by four deeds of transfer all dated 7.12.1989(deed Nos. 4010-4013) who in their turn by different registered deeds transferred the same to different persons including the present respondent Nos. 1 to 21 of Civil Petition for. Leave to Appeal No. 216 of 2008, and accordingly they are in possession of the same.

6. On hearing the parties of both the Miscellaneous cases and on perusal of the materials on record, the Fourth Artharin Adalat, Dhaka, by judgment and order dated 21.5.2005, dismissed both the cases on contest holding that the property in question being not attached the miscellaneous cases under Order XXI Rule 58 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure are mere abuse of the process of the Court; the petitioners failed to prove execution of their title deeds by Md. Fazlul Hoque, the alleged attorney of Dr. Abdul Mannan and on the other hand the execution of the mortgage deed by Abul Hossain, the constituted attorney of Dr. Abdul Mannan, being earlier to the purchase deeds of all the petitioners of both the cases and all such deeds being executed at a point of time when the entire property was under mortgage to the respondent bank and the same being not released from mortgage and that the power of attorney to Abul Hossain having been proved to be genuine and the petitioners having not specifically described their property in the schedule, both the miscellaneous cases are not maintainable.

7. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and order dated 21.5.2005 the present respondent No.1 of Civil Appeal No. 375 of 2009, preferred First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 86 of 2006 before the High Court Division and obtained order of stay of operation of the said judgment and order of the 4th Artharin Adalat, in Civil Rule No. 803(FM) of 2005. Similarly respondent Nos. 1 to 21 of Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 216 of 2008 also preferred First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 145 of 2007 and obtained stay of the operation of the said judgment and order of the 4th Artharin, in Civil Rule No. 795(FM) of 2005.

8. During the pendency of the aforesaid two miscellaneous appeals and the connected civil rules before the High Court Division, the appellants of both the aforesaid two miscellaneous appeals (present respondent Nos. 1 of the Civil Appeal and respondent Nos. 1 to 21 of the civil petition) jointly filed application on 22.12.2005 to the respondent bank expressing their willingness to pay off the decretal amount, if the mortgaged property is released in their favour, on the basis of which, negotiations started between the parties and ultimately the respondent bank, by letter dated 3.9.2009, informed the appellants of both the aforesaid miscellaneous appeals that since they agreed to withdraw the appeals and assumed the liabilities of the decreetal amount of TK.50,00,000/- it had no objection if they pay off the said amount subject to the decision of the Court. After receiving the said letter the appellants of both the miscellaneous appeals filed two applications before the appellate Court for disposal of both the said miscellaneous appeals with direction upon the respondent bank to release the mortgaged property on accepting TK.50,00,000/= and as per direction of the Court the appellants filed applications stating that they had purchased 14 Pay Orders of different banks in favour of the respondent bank for a sum of TK.50,00,000/= and accordingly they are ready to hand over the same to Mr. ASM Abdur Razzaque the learned Advocate for the respondent bank and thereby sought necessary directions.

9. Mr. ASM Abdur Razzaque, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent bank before the High Court Division, admitted that the parties have reached to an agreement outside Court and the bank has no objection to release the mortgaged property in favour of the appellants of the two miscellaneous appeals since they have agreed to pay TK.50,00000/= in full satisfaction of the decreetal amount.

<u>10. Considering the aforesaid facts and circumstances, the High Court Division, by the impugned judgment and order dated 10.12.2007, allowed both the first miscellaneous appeals and disposed of the connected rules upon setting aside the judgment and order dated 21.5.2005 passed by the Fourth Artharin Adalat, Dhaka, in the Miscellaneous Case Nos. 35 and 36 of 2003 and directed the respondent bank to release the mortgaged property and handover the connected title 'deeds, submitted at the time of creating mortgage, which are lying with the respondent bank, in favour of the appellants of both the first miscellaneous appeals.</u>

11. Now the present appellant being the heir of late Dr. Abdul Mannan filed two Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal Nos. 215 and 216 both of 2008 against the impugned judgment and order dated 10.12.2007 passed by the. High Court Division and obtained leave in Civil Petition No. 215 of 2008 which gave rise to Civil Appeal No. 375 of 2009. But Civil Petition No. 216 of 2008 being not moved earlier leave was yet to be granted. Hence, the same is being heard now along with the appeal.

12. Since, the subject matter and the question of law involved in the civil appeal and the civil petition are same, they are taken up together for hearing and disposal.

13. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, the learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant and the petitioner in both the cases submits that as per provision of section 41(1) of the Artharin Adalat Ain, 2003 the miscellaneous appeals filed by the present respondents before the High Court Division are not maintainable since the value of the same is TK.38,91,338.00, which is below TK. 50,00,000/= and as such, the impugned judgment and order is not sustainable in law. He next submits that both the aforesaid miscellaneous appeals were filed without depositing the statutory deposit of 50% of the decreetal amount as required under section 41(1) of the Ain and as such on this score also the same are not maintainable. Lastly, he submits that no order of the Artharin Adalat is entertainable by any Court which is not authorized or empowered under section 20 of the Ain and as such he prayed that the impugned order is liable to be set aside and the appeal is liable to be allowed and the civil petition is also to be disposed of in the light of the appeal.

14. On the other hand, Mr. ASM. Abdur Razzaque, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent bank in both the cases submits that the High Court Division did not commit any illegality n passing the judgment and order as the same are passed on admission/consent of both the parties on the basis of compromise and as such, the same are liable to be affirmed by this Division.

15. To resolve the dispute raised in this appeal and in the civil petition, it is required to see the chronology of events in these two cases. It appears from the record that admittedly the property in question was mortgaged to the National Bank Ltd., the present respondent No.2 of the civil appeal against the loan sanctioned in favour of the present respondent No.3 of the appeal, by Abul Hossain, the constituted attorney of Dr. Abdul Mannan, who was the owner of the property in question, pursuant to the Power of Attorney dated 23.10.1983. But, the present respondent No.3 having failed to repay the loan the respondent bank instituted Title Suit no.177 of 1998 against the present respondent No.3, M/S Cosmopolitan Trading Corporation and Abul Hossen, predecessor of respondent Nos. 4 to 13 for realization of unpaid loan. The said suit was decreed ex parte on 8.4.2001. The plaintiff bank then put the said decree into execution vide Execution C.4se No. 37 of 2002 which on transfer was renumbered as Execution Case No. 1242 of 2003. The present respondent No.1 (Concord Condominium Ltd.) of the civil appeal and respondent No. 1 to 21 of civil petition, having come to know about such decree and about inclusion of their purchased properties in the schedule to the decree filed two Miscellaneous cases being Nos. 35 of 2003 and 36 of 2003, as third party, under Order XXI Rule 58 read with section 151 of the Code narrating their story of purchasing the scheduled property from Dr. Abdul Mannan through his constituted attorney Md. Fazlul Hoque on different dates in 1994 and 1996 which upon hearing all the parties were dismissed on con-test on the ground as stated before. Against the same, the aforementioned First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 86 of 2006 and First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 145 of 2007 were preferred before the High Court Division by the said third party petitioners which were heard and allowed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division by the impugned judgment and order dated 10.12.2007 on the basis of settlement/compromise between the said third party petitioners and the bank. Against the said compromise/consented judgment and order the present appellant of civil appeal and the petitioner of the civil petition, (son of late Dr. Abdul Mannan, the original owner of the scheduled property) who was respondent No.14 in the miscellaneous appeals preferred these two civil appeals and the civil petition.

<u>16. On perusal of the impugned judgment it appears that the High Court Division observed that on the basis of settlement/ compromise between the appellants of the two miscellaneous appeals and the respondent bank and the appellants of both the miscellaneous appeals having paid TK.50,00,000/= by fourteen cheques in full satisfaction of the decretal amount to the respondent bank and the decree holder respondent bank,(who put the decree, into execution), having admitted that the parties have reached to an agreement out of Court and it has no objection to release the mortgaged property in favour of the said appellants pursuant to letter dated 03.09.2006' and as such the High Court Division allowed both the miscellaneous appeals. It also held that 'in view of the liquidation of the entire debts by the said appellant-purchasers as per demand of the respondent bank, we find no legal bar on the part of the respondent bank in releasing the mortgaged property in favour of the third party appellants'.</u>

17. After the loan amount and the demand of the respondent bank has been met by the third party-purchasers, Mohammad Zahangir Alam, son of judgment debtor late Dr. Abdul Mannan, who has been added as judgment debtor in the execution case in place of his late father filed this appeal and the civil petition before this Division challenging the aforesaid consented judgment and order passed by the High Court Division and thereby raising the question as noted in the submission of the learned advocate for the appellant/ petitioner.

<u>18. It is true that against the judgment and decree of the Artharin Adalat none, including the aggrieved party took any step. If an appeal against the decree was to be filed it ought to have been filed before the District Judge if the decretal amount is less than TK.50,00,000/= and if it is higher than TK.50,00,000 then before the High Court Division, of course upon depositing 50% of the decretal amount in either of the cases, as provided in section 41 of the Artharin Adalat Ain. In the present cases it appears that both the aforesaid first miscellaneous appeals were filed by the present respondents as third party-purchaser who purchased the properties in question from the original owner Dr. Abdul Mannan and in the said two miscellaneous appeals the present appellant and his mother (heirs of late Dr. Abdul Mannan) were made respondents Nos. 14 and 13 respectively. It further appears that the said two miscellaneous appeals were preferred against the judgment and order dated 21.5.2005 passed in Miscellaneous Case Nos. 36 and 35 both of 2003, filed under Order XXI Rule 58 read with section 151 of the Code, not, against the original judgment and decree dated 8.4.2001 of the Artha Rin Adalat. The aforesaid respondent Nos. 13 and 14 (of whom respondent No. 14 is the present appellant) being the widow and the son of late Dr. Abdul Mannan respectively, who exhausted his entire share by transfer to some persons from whom the present respondents of both the cases ultimately purchased the same and also by appointing Abul Hossain (predecessor of present respondents No. 4 to 13 of the civil appeal and respondent Nos. 24 to 33 in the civil petition) as his attorney to deal with the said property, accordingly and pursuant to such power dated 23.10.1983, the said attorney, Abul Hossain, mortgaged the same to the respondent bank against the loan sanctioned to respondent No.3. But the present appellant and his mother being parties in the said proceeding and having not challenged the same at any stage now has come before this Division to challenge the impugned order by which a consented judgment and order has been passed.</u>

19. When the parties to an action has expressly and by implication waived or has foregone the right and has come to a consensus to resolve the dispute by any lawful agreement or compromise or even by conduct, they/he cannot challenge such action/order on the ground of acquiescence, waiver and estoppel as well as such order having been passed where he was a party and never raised any objection rather on consent of both the parties, he cannot now raise any objection of pecuniary jurisdiction specially when he kept silent throughout the proceeding and specially when the order has been passed on coin-promise between all other parties and now by preferring this appeal he cannot for the first time raise this issue. In a case reported in 1993 MLR 247=PLD 1984 Quetta 92 it has been held 'where the appeal lay to the District Judge but was filed in the High Court and no objection was raised by the respondent in respect of the procedure and raised only when the decision went against him that irregular mode adopted by the High Court in entertaining the appeal had not resulted in prejudicing the merit of the case. Therefore, the decision of the High Court did not merit reversal.' Though the general principle is 'if the Court has no jurisdiction, no amount of waiver or consent can confer jurisdiction on the Court' but, a distinction must be made between "patent" and "latent" want of jurisdiction, in one, submission to the jurisdiction cannot cure the defect, while in the other, no objection to want of juris-diction can be taken at a later stage if the objection is not taken at the earliest (Altaf Hossain Vs. Chief Settlement Commissioner 18 DLR(SC)164). Again in the case of Sharafat Vs. Dr. Islamuddin (1998 BLD 92) it has been held that 'when a case has been decided on merit, it should not be reversed unless it has resulted in failure of justice'. In the case of Kiran Singh Vs. Chaman (A 1954 SC 340 1 SCR 117) it has been observed that a case tried on merits Should not be liable to be reversed purely on technical grounds, unless it has resulted in failure of justice, and the policy of the legislature has been to treat objections to jurisdiction, both territorial and pecuniary, as technical". Under the Indian jurisdiction, in a series of decisions, it has been held 'when a case is disposed of on merit, no interference by the Appellate or Revisional Court on technical ground of territorial and pecuniary jurisdiction is called for unless prejudiced (AIR 1983 Mad 9). In AIR 1984 Punj 345 it has been held 'lack of pecuniary jurisdiction is no inherent lack of jurisdiction.' Apart from the aforementioned series of decisions on the question of lack of jurisdiction it appears that the predecessor of the present appellant having transferred his entire share in the property in question by registered instruments, his heir, the appellant, cannot now challenge the same before this Division after 25 years of keeping the property under mortgage to the bank against a loan or by transfer without proving his title and possession over the suit land.

20. From the facts and circumstances and the law discussed above, it is clear that the present appellant was a party in the execution proceeding as well as in the appeal who did not raise any objection anywhere before any Court in respect of his right or claim. Even when the purchasers from his father settled the dispute, by compromise with the decree holder bank and the appeals were disposed of in terms of the said compromise to the satisfaction of the decree holder bank, the present appellant did not raise objection.

<u>21. In respect of submission of Mr. Bhuiyan on non-depositing 50% of the decreetal dues as provided under section 41(2) of the Ain it is to be mentioned that section 41 provides preferring appeal against decree or order passed by the Artharin Adalat and in such case the aggrieved party may prefer appeal upon depositing 50% of the decreetal dues if he acknowledges such claim. But in case the aggrieved party does not acknowledge such claim he is to deposit such amount as security in the Adalat which passed the decree otherwise the appeal under section 41(5) will not be in effect accepted. Such pre-condition has also been incorporated in section 19 of the Ain which has provided remedy against exparte decree. But under this section the amount to be deposited is 10% of the decreetal dues. Both these two provisions are in respect of remedy against decree passed in the suit which are not at all applicable in the cases in hand since the decree, either contested or exparte have been challenged. Rather the third party purchasers have filed the miscellaneous cases under Order XXI Rule 58 of the Civil Procedure Code since there was no such provision in the Ain earlier, and there is no such provision of depositing money. Section 6 of the Ain provides applicability of the provisions of the Code which not inconsistent with the AM. In the Artharin Ain of 2003, which came into force from 1st of May 2003, in section 32 has provided remedy against execution wherein under subsection 2 the provision of depositing 25% equal to decreetal amount has been inserted. So prior to that there was no necessity of depositing any amount for challenging the execution proceeding. From the aforesaid provisions of the Ain reading with the pre-amble of the same it appears that the Arthain Adalat Ain 2003 or the earlier Ain of 1999 has been enacted for the purpose of realization/recovery of loans by the financial institutions. The intention of the legislature is very clear. When it appeared that the borrowers of such loans are in the habit of not repaying back the same the legislature enacted such law to compel such defaulting borrowers who has developed a loan defaulting culture, to pay off the loan or to face the consequence of losing their property mortgaged against such loan. And as such the lending bank has been given right to recover the loan along with interests accrued thereon by selling off the property of the defaulting borrower in auction in the execution case filed after the decree.</u>

<u>22. The present cases have arisen out of such execution proceeding which have been filed by the third party purchasers who claimed to have purchased the same from the original owner without notice after the scheduled properties have been mortgaged to the plaintiff-respondent bank. The purpose of enacting laws is to protect the interests of all concerned and as such the present respondents, when came to know that their purchased proper-ties have been included in the schedule of the execution case they filed the miscellaneous cases to protect their purchased property. On the other hand, the financial institutions are also to protect their interests by recovering the unpaid loans by all means. Thus when the third party purchasers came forward to pay off the decreetal dues as per demand of the lending bank and they paid off the same in the two miscellaneous appeals before the High Court Division to the satisfaction of the decree holder bank and none else having come forward to pay off the unpaid loan there is no illegality in passing the impugned judgment and order as the whole purpose of enacting the Ain has been fulfilled which has not resulted in failure of justice.</u>

<u>23. Thus the impugned judgment having been decided on merit and the same having not resulted in failure of justice it is not liable to be reversed. So it is clear that the submissions as advanced by the learned advocate for the appellant in the appeal as well as the petitioner in the civil petition on all points are of no substance.</u>

24. Apart from the aforesaid conduct of the appellant it appears that the appellant did not come with clean hands because he had adequate opportunity to agitate the points raised herein, before the High Court Division and in not doing so and rather after the loan amount as well as the decretal dues having been paid off by the parties to the litigation, who claimed to have purchased the same from his father, to the satisfaction of the decree holder bank this appeal filed by one of the heirs of the original owner, who has exhausted his entire Share much earlier, before this Division is not at all sustainable in law.

<u>25. Thus we find no merit in the submissions of the learned advocate for the appellant as well as for the leave petitioner and as such, this appeal and the leave petition are liable to be dismissed.</u>

<u>26. In the result, this civil appeal is dismissed. Since Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 216 of 2008 has been filed against the same judgment and order of the High Court Division by the same appellant, on the self same grounds, this civil petition is also disposed of in the light of the judgment' passed in the civil appeal. However, there will be no order as to costs.</u>

End.
